prompt: A shop owner runs the same product-description prompt twice in a chat assistant and gets two different openings. She asks whether the assistant is faulty. What does lesson 1 tell her?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 1.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: each word is drawn in proportion to its score, so two runs differ
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It looked up a stored answer, and the stored answers changed between runs
choices.why: There is no lookup: the model scores the next word and one is picked.

choices.text: The second run recalled the first and varied the wording on purpose
choices.why: Nothing carries over between two separate runs; the difference comes from the draw.

choices.text: The prompt was too short; a longer one gives the same text on each run
choices.why: A longer prompt still ends in a draw; taking the top word each time is what repeats.

prompt: An assistant drafting a product page writes, fluently, that a blender "comes with a two-year warranty". Nothing in the material it was given mentions a warranty. Which point from lesson 1 explains how that sentence came about?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 1.

choices.text: Each piece was likely; a fluent sentence needs no fact behind it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The model found the warranty on another shop's page and copied it across
choices.why: The model does not look pages up; it scores what text usually comes next.

choices.text: It was reading a part of the prompt that had fallen outside its window
choices.why: Text outside the window has no effect at all, so it cannot be where a sentence came from.

choices.text: The training that turned it into an assistant taught it to answer, and an answer is expected to contain a claim of some kind
choices.why: That later training makes an answer the likely continuation; it does not put facts in.

prompt: A boutique wants its assistant to use a customer's shoe size, given in yesterday's chat, when she comes back today. By lesson 2, what has to happen?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 2.

choices.text: No extra step: the model keeps each customer's earlier conversations
choices.why: The model has no memory between requests; a chat looks continuous because it is resent.

choices.text: In yesterday's chat, tell the model to store the size for her next visit
choices.why: An instruction lasts as long as the request it is in; nothing is stored afterwards.

choices.text: Retrain the model each night on the day's conversations, so that it learns each customer's details
choices.why: Training is not how one customer's detail reaches a reply; resending it in the request is.

choices.text: The application sends the size again, as text, in today's request
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A company budgets a Portuguese customer-service assistant by counting the tokens of an English sample of the same messages. What does lesson 3 warn?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 3.

choices.text: The Portuguese will come to more tokens; measure with the users' own text
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: No change: a token is a word, so both languages count the same
choices.why: A token is a piece of a word; the café's hours took 48 in Portuguese against 41.

choices.text: The Portuguese will come to fewer tokens, as it has fewer characters
choices.why: The Portuguese file was four characters shorter and seven tokens longer.

choices.text: The two counts match once the larger o200k_base vocabulary is used
choices.why: The larger vocabulary narrows the gap and leaves some: 16 tokens against 12.

prompt: A client wants an assistant to handle several small jobs. Which of them does lesson 3 say should go to a program, or have the letters spelt out first? Choose all that apply.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 3.

choices.text: Counting how many times a letter appears in a product code
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Writing a customer's reference word backwards
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Adding up the totals of a day's orders
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Saying whether a review sounds angry or pleased
choices.why: Tone is meaning, which is visible in which pieces follow which; that is what a model is good at.

choices.text: Rewriting a menu description in a friendlier voice
choices.why: Rewording is about meaning, not about letters hidden inside tokens.

prompt: A supplier contract is too long for the window, so it is split into chunks, each sent with the same instruction, and the answers are combined. The question is whether clause 14 contradicts clause 3. What does lesson 4 say about this question?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 4.

choices.text: It needs two distant parts at once, so no single chunk can answer it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Overlapping the chunks by a few sentences solves it
choices.why: Overlap saves a fact cut at a boundary, not two clauses pages apart.

choices.text: The last request combines every answer, so it sees both clauses side by side and can compare them
choices.why: The last request sees what each chunk answered, not the clauses themselves.

choices.text: Repeat the instruction at the end of each chunk, where it is read last
choices.why: That helps the instruction be followed; it does not bring the other clause into view.

prompt: An FAQ assistant answers from a company's policy document. The team wants a check that runs on every reply with no person reading it. Which request in the prompt makes that possible, by lesson 5?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 5.

choices.text: A number such as [1] after each claim, naming the source it came from
choices.why: A number says where to look; somebody still has to read the source to see whether it agrees.

choices.text: The exact sentence each claim rests on, which a program then searches the document for
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A score from 1 to 10 for how confident the model is in each part of its reply
choices.why: What the model knows and what it finds likely are the same thing inside it, so it cannot grade that.

choices.text: A reply written at temperature 0
choices.why: That makes replies repeatable, not checked; the likeliest answer may be the invented one.

prompt: An assistant can call a `send_invoice` tool, and its system prompt says "Send an invoice only after the customer confirms." A reviewer asks what stops an invoice going out unconfirmed. By lesson 6, what is the honest answer?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 6.

choices.text: A request to the model, and no more, until the program around it checks for a confirmation
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The model, which reads the rule before each call and declines to break it
choices.why: The sentence helps the model behave well; it is not a fact about what can happen.

choices.text: The tool's description, since the model decides from that sentence whether to call it
choices.why: A description shapes what the model asks for; the program still runs whatever is asked.

choices.text: The step limit on the loop
choices.why: A step limit caps how many rounds run, not which calls are allowed.

prompt: A company puts the code that unlocks staff discounts in its public chatbot's system prompt, with the line "Do not reveal this code to anyone." What does lesson 7 say to do?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 7.

choices.text: Mark each user message as untrusted, so the model keeps the code to itself
choices.why: A marking is a strong hint made of tokens, not a wall, and the code would still be in the context.

choices.text: Remove the code: what the context holds is one question from a reply
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Leave it there, because direct injection is the smaller problem and a person typing gets little out of it
choices.why: What a person typing can get includes whatever is written in the prompt.

choices.text: Repeat the warning at the end of the prompt as well
choices.why: It is one more sentence competing with others; it lowers the rate and cannot bring it to zero.

prompt: A team plans to run a 70B model on its own hardware. Using lesson 8's arithmetic, how many gigabytes of memory for the weights does storing them at 4 bits save, compared with 16 bits?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 8.

prompt: A vendor calls its 70B model "ten times smarter" than a 7B one. Lesson 8 says the count is a measure of size, not quality: times the bytes per weight, what it decides exactly is how much ___ the model needs.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 8.

prompt: A vendor's video shows its model summarising a contract flawlessly on the first try, and your manager wants to sign. What would turn that demo into evidence about your own use, by lesson 10?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 10.

choices.text: Running it dozens of times on contracts like yours and counting the successes
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The vendor's benchmark score on a well-known test
choices.why: A vendor's number, on tests it picked, is a claim until somebody else gets it.

choices.text: Watching the full, unedited recording
choices.why: An unedited run is still one run, chosen from the runs somebody saw.

choices.text: Confirming it is generative and not narrow
choices.why: Those words say what kind of system it is, not how often it does your task.

prompt: A model scores 98% on a public test published years ago, and far less on your own tickets. If the test's questions ended up in the text it was trained on, lesson 10 calls that ___.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 10.

prompt: An HR assistant built on keyword retrieval answers "the handbook does not say" to "how much time off do I get for a funeral?". The handbook has a section headed "Bereavement leave". What happened, by lesson 11?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 11.

choices.text: The model ignored its sources and answered from general knowledge
choices.why: Saying the handbook does not say is following the instruction, not ignoring it.

choices.text: The "does not say" line is too strict, and removing it would fix this
choices.why: With no passage in the prompt, the model would write a likely policy, not the company's.

choices.text: The passage came back with a low score and was judged not relevant
choices.why: There is no score that means not relevant; the top passages are returned whatever they are.

choices.text: The question and the passage shared no word, so nothing came back and the model did as told
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Provider A lists a lower price per million input tokens than provider B, and a finance colleague concludes A is cheaper for your Portuguese support assistant. What does lesson 12 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 12.

choices.text: A is cheaper, since a token is the same unit at each provider
choices.why: Even two encodings from one provider gave 11 and 8 tokens for one sentence.

choices.text: Count the words in a typical request and multiply by each price
choices.why: The price is per token, and words do not turn into tokens at a fixed rate.

choices.text: Look up which of the two ranks higher in a recent comparison table
choices.why: A table ranks models on somebody else's tasks, and says nothing of your bill.

choices.text: Compare what a whole typical request costs at each, since each one cuts text into tokens its own way
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Match each job a business gives a model to where lesson 13 says to start the temperature.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 13.

pairs.left: pulling invoice numbers and dates out of scanned forms
pairs.right: 0, or close to it

pairs.left: answering from a policy document pasted into the prompt
pairs.right: low

pairs.left: writing an ordinary explanatory e-mail to a client
pairs.right: the provider's default

pairs.left: suggesting twenty names for a new product line
pairs.right: higher

right_distractors: as high as the API allows

prompt: An extraction prompt leaves open whether "term" in a contract means its duration or a defined word. At temperature 0 it returns the same value in 50 runs out of 50, and the team calls the prompt reliable. What does lesson 13 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 13.

choices.text: It is reliable: fifty identical replies show the prompt is clear
choices.why: Identical replies show the draw was removed, not that the reading chosen is the intended one.

choices.text: Raise the temperature so that both readings come out, and keep it raised in production
choices.why: For extraction, variation is only error; showing both readings does not choose between them.

choices.text: Run it again tomorrow, as hosted models are not deterministic at 0
choices.why: That is true and beside the point: the same reply every time is still one unchosen reading.

choices.text: Temperature 0 picks one reading each time and hides the others; the fix is in the prompt
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Replies occasionally go strange at a temperature you otherwise like. In one edit you set top-p to 0.9 and lower the temperature, and the replies improve. What does lesson 14 say about that edit?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 14.

choices.text: Top-p did the work, since the temperature does not affect what top-p keeps
choices.why: Temperature reshapes the shares before top-p measures them, so it changes the nucleus.

choices.text: The lower temperature did the work, as top-p takes effect only when top-k is set alongside it
choices.why: Top-p acts on its own; with both set, toylm keeps whichever set is smaller.

choices.text: It is sound practice, since the two are separate dials
choices.why: They act on the same list one after another, which is why they do not add up simply.

choices.text: Two things changed at once, so you cannot tell which helped
choices.why: Right.

prompt: An app asks a model to list the items of a customer's order for a confirmation e-mail, with a low output limit to save money. Some e-mails quietly leave out the last items. By lesson 15, what should the code do?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 15.

choices.text: Raise the limit until no e-mail is cut, then stop checking
choices.why: "The largest reply you expect" is a guess, so the finish reason still has to be read.

choices.text: Read the finish reason and treat `length` as a failure
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Check each e-mail against a schema for a list of items, which catches a list cut short
choices.why: A list cut after an item is still a well-formed list; a cut answer rarely looks cut.

choices.text: Ask the model in the prompt to keep within the limit
choices.why: The model never learns a limit existed; it writes as it would have and is stopped.

prompt: A team drops "in one sentence" from a summarising prompt and relies on an output limit of 40 tokens. Lesson 15 says asking for brevity changes what the model writes, while the limit only changes where the reply is ___.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 15.

prompt: A program decides a reply is complete when it ends in `</answer>`. The team also sets `</answer>` as a stop sequence, to save tokens, and the program now reports each reply as incomplete. What does lesson 16 explain?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 16.

choices.text: A stop matched as plain text fired inside a longer word partway through each reply
choices.why: `</answer>` is long and distinctive; a short stop like `at` is the one that fires inside words.

choices.text: The stop text is left out of the output, so the program has to add it back
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The finish reason became `length`, which marks a reply as cut
choices.why: A stop sequence ends with the reason `stop`, not `length`.

choices.text: Stops are matched before the model writes, so the closing tag is never generated at all
choices.why: The loop checks what was written; the token that triggered the stop was generated and counted.

prompt: A catalogue generator kept repeating the same bullet, so someone set a high presence penalty on every request the team sends, including the ones that ask for JSON. The JSON replies are now malformed. What does lesson 17 say happened?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 17.

choices.text: The penalty works by raising the temperature, which loosened the format
choices.why: A penalty subtracts from the scores of used words; temperature is a separate step after it.

choices.text: The penalty told the model to be more varied, and it varied the field names to obey
choices.why: The model receives no instruction; a penalty is arithmetic on the scores.

choices.text: A presence penalty acts only on prose, and leaves the punctuation and brackets of a structured reply alone
choices.why: It lowers the score of each word already in the output, whatever that word is.

choices.text: JSON has to repeat quotes and braces, and the penalty pushed those down
choices.why: Right.

prompt: In lesson 17's `the cat` loop at temperature 0, `and` leads `on` by about 0.41 after `cat sleeps`. With a frequency penalty of 0.1, no other control and no token limit in the way, how many times will `and` have been written when `on` first wins?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 17.

prompt: A model exports a shop's sales as CSV, with prices written the Brazilian way, `18,50`. The import into the finance system reports no error, and the week's totals come out wrong. What does lesson 18 point to?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 18.

choices.text: A CSV reader stops on a malformed row, so the fault is in the finance system's arithmetic
choices.why: The reader takes rows of four fields without complaint; CSV allows them.

choices.text: Ask for a Markdown table, which keeps the columns apart
choices.why: Markdown is for people: it has no fixed fields and can be written in several ways.

choices.text: Fields split at their own comma; count each row's fields against the header
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Ask the model to double-check its quoting before it replies
choices.why: A model applies quoting less reliably than a library; the check is yours to write.

prompt: A tag extractor finds no `<label>` in a reply that ends "Label: negative" and exits with status 1. A colleague wants it to fall back to taking the reply's last word. What does lesson 18 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 18.

choices.text: Add the fallback, since it returns the right label for this reply
choices.why: It works here and returns `staff.` on the next reply that puts its label first.

choices.text: Switch to Markdown, since a heading is easier for a program to find than a tag
choices.why: Markdown has no fixed fields, and the same look can be written several ways underneath.

choices.text: Keep the failure: an extractor that says it found nothing is right
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Treat exit status 1 as the label `neutral`
choices.why: That turns a missing answer into an invented one that looks like data.

prompt: The provider now offers a structured-output mode that keeps each reply valid against your schema. A manager proposes deleting the rules check and the review of replies against their inputs. What does lesson 19 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 19.

choices.text: Delete them, since a reply that fits the schema is one the program can trust
choices.why: Constrained decoding makes the category one of five words, not the right one of the five.

choices.text: Keep only the retry loop, which sends the errors back until the values come right
choices.why: A valid reply with a wrong value produces no error message to send back.

choices.text: Delete the rules and keep a person reading each reply
choices.why: Rules are a cheap program layer that stops what the schema passes; dropping them wastes the person's time.

choices.text: Keep them: a reply can fit the schema and still be wrong
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A customer was charged R$ 140 instead of R$ 70, and the triage reply puts 140 in `refund_amount`. It passes the schema, and `rules.py` flags it only for the manager's approval. Which check would have caught the wrong amount, by lesson 19?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 19.

choices.text: A schema with `"maximum": 100` on the refund amount
choices.why: The amount owed could be any number; a schema never sees the complaint.

choices.text: A check that the refund amount is one of the amounts the complaint mentions
choices.why: Both 70 and 140 are in the complaint, so 140 would pass.

choices.text: Constrained decoding with the same schema, so that the model can only write valid values for each field
choices.why: 140 is already a valid value; the mode makes replies fit the shape, not match the input.

choices.text: One that reads the complaint and the reply side by side
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A one-shot prompt for sorting support e-mails has a single example: a long, angry message about a refund, labelled `refund`. Replies come back labelled `refund` too often. What does lesson 21 say is going on?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 21.

choices.text: Its label, length and topic all read as the pattern; cover every class
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A single example sits too far from the message, so the model cannot see it
choices.why: A large model sees the whole prompt; the example reached it and is being copied.

choices.text: Examples fix the form of the answer and not which label is chosen, so the cause lies in the description
choices.why: Examples also show where a boundary falls, which is why a sarcastic one moved the label.

choices.text: The example is too emotional, and a neutral one would be followed less
choices.why: Tone is one of the things it teaches, but a calm `refund` example alone would lean the same way.

prompt: At lesson 21's illustrative prices, 10,000 messages cost 4.50 with `prompt-few.txt` and 2.38 with `prompt-zero.txt`. A shop expects 1,000,000 messages. How much more would the four examples cost over those messages, in the same units?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 21.

prompt: A shop's assistant has a short system prompt. The owner wants this week's opening hours and specials added to it, "so the assistant always knows them". What does lesson 22 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 22.

choices.text: Leave them out: facts that change arrive with each question
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Add them, since the system message is the one place the model treats as authoritative
choices.why: Its weight is trained, and a fact that changes weekly is not a standing instruction.

choices.text: Put them in the first user message of each conversation instead
choices.why: There it is one message among many, in the same voice as the customer's questions.

choices.text: Add them at the end of the system prompt, where they are read last and so are easiest for the model to recall
choices.why: Position helps an instruction be followed; it does not make a weekly fact a standing one.

prompt: A furniture shop's assistant is asked whether a sofa's fabric is waterproof. Its prompt now opens "You are a world-class textile scientist. Answer with authority." and its replies sound far more convincing. What does lesson 23 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 23.

choices.text: The role changed the tone and added no facts; send the product sheet with the question
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The answers are now more reliable, since the role draws on the expert part of the model's training
choices.why: The model knows what it knew before the line; nothing it says becomes truer.

choices.text: Swap it for the role of the shop's own salesperson
choices.why: A different role changes the voice again; the facts about this sofa are still missing.

choices.text: Keep the role and add "be sure of your facts"
choices.why: The model cannot tell which of its likely answers are false, so the line adds nothing.

prompt: You are about to ask a model to draft a reply to a supplier who says a delivery was refused at your door. How does lesson 24 suggest finding the context your prompt is missing?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 24.

choices.text: Picture a temp on their first morning, with no chance to ask; what they would ask is missing
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Send the bare request and add whatever facts the reply gets wrong
choices.why: A gap is filled with the usual answer, and nothing in a fluent reply shows it was invented.

choices.text: Paste the supplier's whole file, so the model has it all
choices.why: Unrelated text costs tokens on each request and gives the reply more to wander into.

choices.text: Open with a role for the model, such as an experienced logistics manager who has handled many disputes
choices.why: A role sets the voice; it brings none of the facts of this delivery.

prompt: A two-call step-back prompt answers a returns question wrongly, and the final answer follows neatly from the rules the first call listed. Where does lesson 25 tell you to look?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 25.

choices.text: At the second call's prompt, since a wrong answer means the question was worded badly there
choices.why: The second call answered faithfully from what it was given; the wrong principle came earlier.

choices.text: At the first reply, checking each rule it states against the policy
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: At the temperature of the second call
choices.why: The answer follows logically from the rules; the draw is not where it went wrong.

choices.text: No need to look: an answer that follows from its rules is correct
choices.why: A plausible rule that is not in the policy gives a logical answer that is still wrong.

prompt: Lesson 25 contrasts two techniques that write something before the answer: chain of thought writes the steps from this question to its answer, and a step back writes the general ___ that the question is an instance of.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 25.

prompt: A pricing assistant asks for the working step by step and a last line starting `Answer:`. Some replies reach the program with no `Answer:` line at all, ending mid-step. What does lesson 26 point to?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 26.

choices.text: The model judged those questions too simple to need a final line
choices.why: The reply stops mid-step, which is what a limit does, not a choice about the format.

choices.text: The program should take the last number in the reply as the answer
choices.why: A chain is full of numbers; a missing marker means the reply failed.

choices.text: Asking for the steps confuses parsers, so the instruction to think step by step should be removed from the prompt
choices.why: The fixed `Answer:` line exists exactly so a program can parse a chain.

choices.text: An output limit set for short answers cut the chain off
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A lender's manager wants to show an auditor the model's chain of thought as the record of how each application was decided. What does lesson 26 say about that use?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 26.

choices.text: It is sound, as the answer is predicted from those steps and so they show the real reasoning
choices.why: A model can write tidy steps that lead to an answer it was going to give anyway.

choices.text: The steps are not a faithful account of how the answer came about
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is sound once each step's arithmetic has been checked
choices.why: A chain with correct arithmetic in each line still invented a rule in lesson 26.

choices.text: It is sound for reasoning models, since their chain is produced before the answer
choices.why: Being written first does not make the steps an account of how the answer was reached.

prompt: A team wants self-consistency to choose the best one-paragraph summary of each complaint: five samples, then a vote. What does lesson 27 say will happen?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 27.

choices.text: Each vote is a tie of ones, since no two paragraphs match
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The summary most of the samples agree with in meaning wins
choices.why: The vote compares final answers as strings; it cannot see meaning.

choices.text: It works once the samples are drawn at temperature 0, so they come out alike
choices.why: At 0 the five are copies, and a vote among copies is no vote.

choices.text: The longest summary wins, as it shares the most words with the other samples
choices.why: The vote counts identical answers; shared words are not counted at all.

prompt: A team plans to use tree of thoughts to write customer replies: propose several first paragraphs, judge them, keep the best, and continue. What does lesson 28 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 28.

choices.text: It suits replies well, since each paragraph is a state that leads towards the finished text
choices.why: A state helps only if it can be judged against constraints, and a partial reply cannot.

choices.text: Raise the breadth so that more paragraphs survive each level
choices.why: Breadth insures against a wrong judge; here there is no judgement to insure.

choices.text: A first paragraph cannot be judged, so there is nothing to prune by
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It costs about the same as a single chain of thought
choices.why: A tree takes a call per proposal and per judgement; a chain takes one.

prompt: A ReAct trace ends `done`. One Observation says a refund above R$ 100 needs the manager, the calculator returned 111.6, and the answer says no approval is needed. The last Thought reads "That is a normal refund." What does lesson 29 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 29.

choices.text: A stop sequence on `Observation:` would have prevented this
choices.why: That stops the model inventing an observation; here it ignored a real one.

choices.text: The loop would have refused an answer that contradicts an observation, so the trace was edited
choices.why: A turn with an `Answer:` is all the loop looks for; it cannot check the reasoning.

choices.text: Raise the step limit so that the model has room to reconsider
choices.why: The run ended with an answer, not at its limit; more steps change nothing.

choices.text: The loop checks only the shape; the evidence is there for a person or a second check
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Which of these failures does the loop itself stop or refuse, by lesson 29? Choose all that apply.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 29.

choices.text: An Action written with round brackets instead of square ones
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A call to `send_email` in a task whose allow-list does not hold it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A run that reaches its step limit with no answer
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: An answer that contradicts an observation two lines above it
choices.why: The loop prints `done` for any turn with an answer; the evidence waits for a reader.

choices.text: A thought that cites no fact at all
choices.why: The loop reads Actions and Answers; what a thought says is not checked.

prompt: Your team calls a model only through a hosted API. To cut prompt costs, someone proposes prompt tuning: train a soft prompt and stop sending the long written one. What does lesson 30 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 30.

choices.text: Train it once, then send the vectors in place of the written prompt
choices.why: There is no field in an API request where a vector could go.

choices.text: It works if you translate the trained vectors back into the nearest words
choices.why: The nearest tokens do not read as an instruction, since the vectors were never those words.

choices.text: It is closed to you: an API takes text, and there are no weights to train against
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It works, but the soft prompt has to be retrained whenever the written prompt is edited
choices.why: The obstacle comes first: without the weights the training cannot run at all.

prompt: An automatic prompt search scores candidates by exact match on the first word. A reply of `sweet` was scored wrong, though the source text says it, because the label listed `gone`. What does lesson 31 say to do?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 31.

choices.text: Check the metric on a few replies by hand before trusting a ranking built on it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Keep it: exact match is the strictest metric, so its winner is the safest
choices.why: Strict is not the same as right: it scored a correct reply as wrong.

choices.text: Have a model grade each reply instead
choices.why: A grading model has preferences of its own; it still needs checking by hand.

choices.text: Score more candidates, so the metric's mistakes even out
choices.why: The search optimises what the metric rewards; more candidates push harder towards `gone`.

prompt: A prompt search tries a hundred candidates on a dozen examples and finds one that looks excellent on those twelve and does worse on new inputs. Lesson 31's general name for a choice like that is ___.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 31.

prompt: A shop's chat assistant keeps losing what customers said early in long conversations, because old turns are cut to fit the budget. Put lesson 4's fix, a note carried forward, in the order the application runs it.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 4.
items: Find the oldest turns that will no longer fit the budget
Send them to a second, cheaper request that writes down what the customer said about themselves and any promise made
Put that note in the part of the request that is never cut, beside the system prompt
Drop the old turns and send the note with the newest turns that fit
trap: The note is written while the old turns are still there: once they are dropped, nothing is left to summarise.

prompt: You support several teams that use a model. Match each job to the technique the course's last lessons point to as the cheapest one that works for it.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 28.

pairs.left: the price of a flat white, read off the menu
pairs.right: a direct prompt, with no steps asked for

pairs.left: an order total with a loyalty rule applied before the sum
pairs.right: one chain of thought ending in an `Answer:` line

pairs.left: a yes-or-no refund decision where a wrong answer costs more than a few extra calls
pairs.right: several sampled chains and a vote on the final answer

pairs.left: a staff rota puzzle where an early choice can lead into a dead end, and each partial rota can be checked
pairs.right: a search that judges partial steps and drops the weak ones

right_distractors: a role line naming the model an expert in the field

prompt: A manager estimates the monthly bill for a customer chat assistant by pricing one sample question and its reply, then multiplying by the expected number of messages. Which of these will make the real bill larger than that estimate, by lesson 3? Choose all that apply.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 3.

choices.text: The tenth message of a chat sends the nine before it again, as input
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A long system prompt goes out with each request
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: No output limit was set, so the model decides how long each reply is
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The model keeps each conversation between visits, and that memory is billed as stored tokens
choices.why: The model keeps nothing between requests; what it recalls was sent again as input.

choices.text: Output tokens are priced below input tokens, so long replies were overestimated
choices.why: On the large providers' price lists an output token costs more than an input one.

prompt: At lesson 9's illustrative input price of 2.50 per million, `few-shot.txt` sends 165 input tokens. A model fine-tuned on the task would need only `short.txt`'s 13, but suppose its provider bills the tuned model's input at 7.50 per million. Ignoring output, by how much does the input bill shrink over 1,000,000 requests, in the same units?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 9.

prompt: Two support leads label the same 40 tickets by hand for a new labelling prompt, and they disagree on 6 of them. What does lesson 20 make of those 6?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 20.

choices.text: Noise, to be removed so that the test set stays clean
choices.why: Those are exactly the inputs where a reasonable reader could go either way.

choices.text: Cases to leave to the model, which will settle them more consistently than two people
choices.why: The model has no way to guess your decision; it fills the gap with what is likely.

choices.text: Each is a decision the prompt has to state
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A sign that 40 tickets are too few, so label 400 before writing anything
choices.why: More tickets bring more of the same disagreement until somebody decides.

prompt: A change to a café website assistant's system prompt is about to ship. Which of these belong in the test set it is run against first, by lesson 22? Choose all that apply.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 22.

choices.text: A question inside the assistant's scope
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A question outside it, such as one about the weather
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: An allergen question the handbook cannot answer
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A request for a refund
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The examples already written into the prompt
choices.why: A test that holds the prompt's own examples scores well for the wrong reason.

choices.text: The questions customers praised the answers to last month
choices.why: Easy cases score each version well and say nothing about what the change broke.

prompt: An assistant that reads supplier e-mails needs a `place_order` tool, and each call is held until a buyer confirms it. A colleague suggests showing the buyer the model's explanation of why it wants the order, instead of the order itself, "since it's easier to read". What does lesson 7 say?
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 7.

choices.text: Show the order itself, which an injection cannot disguise
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Show the explanation, since it says why the order makes sense
choices.why: That is the model's account, and an injected e-mail can shape it.

choices.text: Drop the hold and mark each supplier e-mail as untrusted instead, so the buyer is not slowed down by approvals
choices.why: A marking is a hint to the model; the hold is what still stands after it is fooled.

choices.text: Show both, and let the model mark which one the buyer should trust
choices.why: A fooled model's advice about what to trust is part of what was fooled.

prompt: A refund assistant draws five sampled chains for each case and votes on the final answer. Match each outcome of the vote to what lesson 27 says the program should do with it.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 27.

pairs.left: `refund` in 5 of 5
pairs.right: accept the answer

pairs.left: `refund` 3, `replace` 2
pairs.right: send it to a person or a second round of samples

pairs.left: `refund`, `replace` and `voucher` once each
pairs.right: treat the case as hard for this prompt

pairs.left: a reply with no answer line
pairs.right: count it as no vote

right_distractors: pick one of the answers at random

prompt: Your manager asks you to choose a model for the company's ticket summaries. Put lesson 12's way of choosing in order.
hint: Prompt Engineering, lesson 12.
items: Collect twenty to fifty real tickets, each with the summary you would accept
Run each candidate on that same set and count the acceptable summaries
Price a whole typical request at each model that did well enough
Pick the cheapest of those
Keep the set, to judge the replacement when that model is retired
trap: Quality comes first: price is compared only among the models that do the task well enough.

prompt: A property manager's prompt sorts tenant messages into `plumbing`, `electrical` and `billing`. You add one example: a dispute over a plumber's invoice, labelled `billing`. Now *the plumber never came on Tuesday* comes back `billing` too. Following lesson 1, which example do you add next?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 1.

choices.text: An obvious billing case, such as a tenant asking for a copy of last month's rent receipt.
choices.why: An obvious case teaches the format and little else; the line between the two labels stays where the first example pushed it.

choices.text: None: delete the invoice example and describe the labels in words instead.
choices.why: Boundary examples are the ones worth their tokens; the fix is a neighbour on the other side, not losing the example.

choices.text: A missed repair appointment, with the label `plumbing`.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: An electrical fault labelled `electrical`, to balance the three labels.
choices.why: Balance matters, but this message is pulled across the plumbing–billing line, and only an example on that line moves it back.

prompt: A client sends 200,000 messages a month through a prompt. Cutting dead lines removes 120 input tokens from every call. At the lab's price of 300 cents per million input tokens, how many cents a month does the cut save?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 2.

prompt: A client's model wraps about one reply in twenty in a code fence, and no wording you try stops it. The developer proposes stripping fences inside the evaluation check so the dashboard stops showing those failures. What does lesson 3 recommend instead?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 3.

choices.text: Keep the check strict, and add a named repair step to the consuming program that counts each time it fires.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Accept the lenient check, since the content inside the fence is right anyway and the router only ever needs the content.
choices.why: A repair inside the measurement hides the thing being repaired, and a later edit that worsens it goes unseen.

choices.text: Retry each fenced reply with the same prompt until one parses.
choices.why: A retry is a fresh chance only when something changes; asking the same question again is not that.

choices.text: Search the fenced text for a label such as `billing` and act on it.
choices.why: That is guessing: a format failure turned into a content decision nobody checked.

prompt: You are reading a client's logs from OpenAI's Chat Completions API. A reply stopped by the output cap is marked with a `finish_reason` of ___.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 6.

prompt: After temperature, five candidates have probabilities 0.50, 0.25, 0.12, 0.08 and 0.05. With top-k 2, what is the probability of the top candidate once the survivors are renormalised? Two decimal places.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 8.

prompt: A developer-tools company's support prompt marks each ticket with triple backticks. Customers paste stack traces and code fences into their tickets, and many come back as `other`. What change does lesson 9 point to?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 9.

choices.text: Tell the model in capitals to ignore any backticks inside the ticket.
choices.why: No wording can stop a fence from closing; the template is what put the structure there.

choices.text: Strip the backticks out of the customer's text first.
choices.why: That changes what the customer wrote, and the person reading the ticket sees a message nobody sent.

choices.text: A named pair of tags around the ticket, with the value escaped.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Switch to four backticks, which customers type less often than three.
choices.why: Still a mark the content can contain, and so a mark the content can close.

prompt: After you add `|xml` escaping, 5 of 40 attack calls still obey an instruction from the customer's message. The client asks: *So escaping did not work?* What is the accurate answer?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 10.

choices.text: It did its job: those five never left the tag, and escaping protects structure, not words.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It did not; switch to triple backticks, which models respect more.
choices.why: Any delimiter has the same property, and backticks are easier for the content to close.

choices.text: It worked, and the five are noise that a second run will remove, since leaks come and go between runs.
choices.why: Five in forty is what a leak rate of about ten in a hundred produces; it does not go away by rerunning.

choices.text: It did not; add a pattern scanner that blocks suspicious messages before they reach the model.
choices.why: Blocking on a scan refused an honest customer and let two instructions through.

prompt: Your client's best few-shot examples are hard boundary messages, which are also the best test cases. What guard does lesson 11 recommend?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 11.

choices.text: Keep them in both places, and subtract one point from the score for each.
choices.why: The inflation depends on how many leaked and how many were failing; a fixed deduction does not measure it.

choices.text: Separate files, and a search before every run that no example message appears among the cases.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Use invented examples in the prompt, since real messages belong only in tests.
choices.why: Lesson 1 says take examples from real traffic; the point is to keep them out of the test set.

choices.text: Rerun at temperature 1 so the copied answers stop matching.
choices.why: Sampling makes the count flaky; it does not stop a prompt from containing its own answers.

prompt: A bank's alert-sorting prompt is re-released with category accuracy up 3 points and one more fraud alert filed as routine. The team ranks versions by a weighted score, which went up. What does lesson 12 recommend?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 12.

choices.text: A gate on missed fraud: the release is refused whatever accuracy did.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Ship it: the weighted score went up, and it is the measure the team agreed on.
choices.why: A single weighted score lets one metric hide another.

choices.text: Raise the weight on fraud recall in the score and recompute both versions.
choices.why: A weight can still be bought back by a gain elsewhere; that is what a gate prevents.

choices.text: Report accuracy alone, which is the number managers understand.
choices.why: Accuracy counts a missed fraud alert exactly like a harmless mistake.

prompt: In a client's confusion matrix, the row for `refund` holds 18 messages: 12 were called `refund`, 4 `billing` and 2 had no usable label. What is the recall for `refund`? Two decimal places.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 12.

prompt: To get the most from the cache, you move a client's customer message from the top of the prompt to the end. Three replies that used to pass now come back in a code fence. What is going on?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 17.

choices.text: The cache returned stored replies from earlier calls.
choices.why: A prompt cache stores the work of reading a prefix, never answers.

choices.text: Nothing to worry about: a cache cannot change the answers.
choices.why: The cache did not change them; the reorder did, and it has to be tested.

choices.text: The reorder is a new prompt; test it like one.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The blocks expired; clearing the cache will fix it.
choices.why: Expiry changes what a call costs, not what it answers.

prompt: A recruitment client asks whether its screening prompt treats candidates differently by name. You run 40 CVs signed *Maria Souza* and the same 40 signed *John Smith*: 3 answers differ, in no consistent direction. Running the Maria file twice also gives 3 differences. What do you report?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 18.

choices.text: A name bias of 3 in 40, to be fixed before launch.
choices.why: Three differ between two runs of the same file too; that is the floor, not a finding.

choices.text: Nothing above the noise floor; widen the set to more names.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Evidence that the prompt is fair to candidates whatever their name.
choices.why: Two names are one comparison; a bias against a group shows only when the group is in the set.

choices.text: That the test is invalid, because CVs carry more than a name.
choices.why: The copies differ only in the name, which is what makes it a counterfactual test.

prompt: Your script sends 300 requests to a model provider's API as fast as it can. Some come back *not now*, and the script resends each failure at once, in a loop with no limit. What does lesson 1 say about that loop?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 1.

choices.text: Put a limit in the loop and wait a little longer before each attempt.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is the right instinct: an immediate retry clears a refusal fastest, before others take the slot.
choices.why: If the server is struggling, clients retrying at once are the load that keeps it down.

choices.text: Open more connections, so each one is answered sooner.
choices.why: That adds load to a server already refusing; it is the same mistake, wider.

choices.text: Treat the refusal as a broken server and stop using the API.
choices.why: A server refusing you quickly may be a server working correctly.

prompt: A client's site shows AI-written Portuguese product descriptions with question marks and boxes where the accented letters should be. Lesson 6's rule for the `Content-Type` of text in a language with accents: say `charset=___`.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

prompt: A client pastes a vendor's AI chat widget into the `<head>` as a plain `<script src=...>`. On days the vendor's host is slow, the whole site shows a blank screen. What does lesson 10 suggest?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 10.

choices.text: Wait for the `load` event before showing anything on the page.
choices.why: `load` waits for everything, the slow widget included; the visitor would wait longer.

choices.text: Move the widget's stylesheet to the end of the body, where it no longer blocks rendering.
choices.why: What stops the parser here is the script, fetched and run before parsing continues.

choices.text: Load it with `async`, so the parser does not wait on another company's host.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Ask the vendor for a minified build of the widget, so that the block is shorter.
choices.why: The block lasts as long as the vendor's host takes to answer; a smaller file on a slow host still stops the parser.

prompt: A client's page with an AI widget feels slow. Put lesson 11's steps for finding out why in order.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 11.
items: Open the network panel
Reload the page with the panel open
Sort the rows by time
Click the slowest row and open its timing
Read which bar is the biggest before deciding the fix
trap: Reloading before the panel is open records nothing: it records only from the moment it opens.

prompt: A client asks whether its support prompt gives a lower urgency to messages written in informal Portuguese than to the same messages written formally. Put the steps of lesson 18's test in order.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 18.
items: Make a copy of each message that differs only in register
Diff the two files to confirm nothing else changed
Run the same file twice to find the noise floor
Run both files with the same prompt and settings
Compare the answers and look for a direction above the floor
trap: Comparing before the noise floor is known reads ordinary variation between runs as a finding about register.

prompt: A client's router sometimes receives a reply that does not parse. Put lesson 3's handling of such a reply in order.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 3.
items: Parse the reply strictly
Call once more, sending the failed reply and the parser's complaint
If it still fails, send the raw reply and the message to a person
Add the message, with a person's answer, to the test set
trap: Resending the same prompt asks the same question again; the retry worth trying first is a different prompt, with the complaint in it.

prompt: You propose raising a client's `max_tokens` from 60 to 120, because a new field pushed ordinary replies close to 60. Their finance lead objects that this doubles the bill. What does lesson 6 say?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 6.

choices.text: Right: keep 60 and ask for shorter answers in the prompt instead.
choices.why: The bill is for tokens written, and a cap that ordinary replies reach cuts them into failures.

choices.text: It raises the input bill, since the cap travels with every request and is counted as prompt.
choices.why: The cap is a setting, not text the model reads; it adds no tokens to the prompt.

choices.text: It makes every reply longer, since the model writes until it reaches the cap.
choices.why: The cap is where writing stops if it gets that far; a reply that finishes earlier ends with `end`.

choices.text: Nothing on a reply that stops before the cap: what is charged is the tokens written.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A client wants each customer's last five messages, free text full of commas and line breaks, placed in the prompt as context. Which input format does lesson 7 point to?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 7.

choices.text: A table with a header row, which pays for its column names once and is the cheapest per record.
choices.why: Values with commas and line breaks break a table's columns.

choices.text: Plain sentences, the cheapest form and the one a model reads most naturally.
choices.why: Prose is the hardest to keep consistent, and a missing field in it is hard to notice.

choices.text: JSON, which says exactly where each value ends.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whichever has fewest tokens, since the model reads the facts the same way.
choices.why: Real models are sensitive to format; choose one a model and a person can both read, then measure.

prompt: A client's prompt change broke exactly one message, and every other message that changed was fixed. How many fixed messages does the sign test need before p falls below 0.05?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 7.

prompt: Since the client's prompt moved to tags, five of the six pasted-message cases pass. A colleague proposes deleting all six from the test set, since they have done their job. What does lesson 9 say?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 9.

choices.text: Delete the five that pass and keep the one that still fails.
choices.why: The five that pass are what would catch an edit that brings the backticks back.

choices.text: Move them into the prompt as examples, where they teach the model the right boundary.
choices.why: A test case that is also an example is answered by copying, and measures nothing.

choices.text: Keep them: a regression test, so the failure cannot come back unnoticed.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Delete them: six cases are too few for a sign test to say anything.
choices.why: Here the evidence is in the replies, and each case shows the mechanism.

prompt: A client's engineer insists the customer's text must sit inside `<user_input>` tags, *because that is the tag name models are trained on*. What does lesson 9 say about tag names?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 9.

choices.text: He is right: Anthropic's page on XML tags lists the names that work.
choices.why: The page recommends tags; no particular names are special.

choices.text: Avoid tags altogether, since models read them as HTML and skip what is inside.
choices.why: Models see a great deal of HTML and XML, which is a reason tags work.

choices.text: Use triple backticks instead, which every model knows from Markdown and every reader recognises.
choices.why: Backticks are common in exactly what customers paste, so the content can close them.

choices.text: No name is special; use the tags consistently and name them in the instructions.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A compliance officer asks how seriously the industry ranks prompt injection. You cite the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, which places it ___ on its list.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 10.

prompt: A client builds its test set from the forty messages that arrived last Monday, the day a courier strike hit. What does lesson 11 warn about?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 11.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the messages are real traffic rather than invented ones.
choices.why: Real is necessary and not enough: one day's mix is that day's inbox.

choices.text: Forty is too many for one day; the set should hold one message per category.
choices.why: Forty is already too few for small effects; the trouble is the mix, not the count.

choices.text: Add forty invented messages in the other categories to balance it.
choices.why: Invented messages are tidier than real ones and measure an inbox that does not exist.

choices.text: A set from one bad day is mostly one kind of message; draw from more than one period.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Two support leads label the same 60 messages for a client's test set. They disagree on 7, all of them refunds paid after a return. What does lesson 11 say to do with that?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 11.

choices.text: Ask a third person and take the majority label for each of the seven.
choices.why: That settles seven labels and leaves the rule unwritten, so the prompt meets the same doubt.

choices.text: Treat it as a finding about the categories: write the rule that settles it, and give the prompt that rule.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Drop the seven, since a case people disagree on is noise in the score.
choices.why: Those are the boundary cases, the ones most worth measuring.

choices.text: Run the prompt on them and keep whichever lead's labels it agrees with.
choices.why: Labels chosen after seeing the model's answer are a judgement of whether it is acceptable.

prompt: You are building a first test set for a client's triage prompt. Put lesson 11's steps in order.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 11.
items: Draw messages from the traffic the prompt will see
Remove names, addresses and order numbers, and keep the typos
Write each message's label before the prompt runs on it
Run the prompt and count against the labels
trap: Running the prompt before labelling turns labelling into approving the model's answers.

prompt: A vendor's fraud-flagging prompt is sold to a bank client with one figure: *recall for fraud: 1.00*. What does lesson 12 say to ask for?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 12.

choices.text: Nothing more: for fraud, catching every case is what counts.
choices.why: Recall alone is bought by flagging everything, and the analysts drown.

choices.text: Overall accuracy, which combines recall and precision into one honest figure.
choices.why: Accuracy counts every wrong answer the same; the two are reported per label.

choices.text: Cohen's kappa against the bank's analysts, which corrects the recall for chance agreement.
choices.why: Kappa measures agreement between raters; it does not stand in for a label's precision.

choices.text: The precision too: calling everything fraud would also score 1.00.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A client's safety report shows *honest messages wrongly refused: 0*. Their system has no way to refuse a message at all. How should that line be reported, by lesson 12?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 12.

choices.text: As a strong result: the system never refuses an honest customer.
choices.why: It cannot refuse anybody, so the count could not have been anything else.

choices.text: As proof that the injection defences cost the business nothing in lost customers.
choices.why: A count that cannot move proves nothing about any defence.

choices.text: Removed, since a metric that is always zero adds clutter to the report.
choices.why: It is the number that will tell them when a change makes the product useless; say why it is zero now.

choices.text: As zero by construction, said as such rather than as a result.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A client's tone rules (exclamation marks, length, banned phrases, promises, acknowledgement) pass all 200 replies this week. Which questions have the rules left unanswered? Choose all that apply.
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 12.

choices.text: Whether each reply is true.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether it answers what the customer asked.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether it sounds like somebody who cares.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether it uses more than one exclamation mark.
choices.why: That is a rule the set already checks.

choices.text: Whether it addresses the customer as *valued customer*.
choices.why: A banned phrase; the rules catch it without fail.

prompt: A client calibrated a judge on 20 labelled pairs and got a kappa of 0.35, *fair* on the usual scale. They plan to judge 5,000 replies a week with it. What does lesson 13 say is missing?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 13.

choices.text: Nothing: *fair* agreement is enough for a judge whose verdicts nobody reads.
choices.why: A judge needs a person reading a sample of its verdicts for as long as it is in use.

choices.text: A few hundred labelled pairs first: on 20, one pair moves the agreement by five points.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A switch to raw agreement, which is easier to explain to managers.
choices.why: Raw agreement hides how much of it chance would give.

choices.text: A higher temperature, so that its verdicts spread more evenly.
choices.why: Sampling adds a way to give two answers to one question.

prompt: Reading a client's failure log of twelve entries together, you notice that three of them end *pulled towards the first example's label*. What does lesson 15 make of that?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 15.

choices.text: Something about how the prompt is built, its examples, rather than about three messages.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Three unrelated messages, each closed once its case was added.
choices.why: Read together, entries show patterns no single one does.

choices.text: A sign the log repeats the tests and could be dropped.
choices.why: The tests catch each message; only the log shows what they share.

choices.text: Evidence that the people who labelled those three messages disagreed with each other about the category.
choices.why: The entries name a pull towards an example's label, which is the prompt's doing.

prompt: A client's manager, deciding whether to ship, asks what the triage prompt costs. `pl cost` printed 0.12768 cents a call and 127,680 cents for a million calls. Which figure does lesson 16 put in front of her?
hint: Reliable Prompts: Evaluation and Good Practice, lesson 16.

choices.text: The cost per call, which is the price of one decision.
choices.why: A cost per call sounds like nothing.

choices.text: The token counts, which do not change when the provider changes its prices.
choices.why: Tokens are not money; the decision is about a budget.

choices.text: The 127,680 cents: per call it sounds like nothing; that one is a budget.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The share of the cost that is output.
choices.why: Useful for deciding where to cut, not for deciding whether to ship.

choices.text: `302`, since a temporary redirect is the safe one to start with.

choices.text: Let the purpose set it: a longer raw tier, with the reason written.

choices.text: Keep 30 days: the LGPD sets that as the limit for keeping raw text.

choices.text: Answer the disputes from the redacted tier instead, which keeps 180 days.

choices.text: Put a hold on every raw file, so nothing goes before 90 days.
choices.why: A hold is for a named case with an end date; a blanket hold is an unwritten policy.

choices.text: No entry, since the user has already been told a person will reply.
choices.why: One line per event still goes to the log, with what happened.

choices.text: The traceback, sent to the user as well, so they can report it.

prompt: Your prompt project's page sends a question, and the model takes eight seconds to answer. For those eight seconds the page shows nothing at all. Which state is missing?

choices.text: Error
choices.why: Nothing failed; the answer is on its way.

choices.text: Loading
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: None, as the reply does arrive in the end
choices.why: On a slow connection this is the state people see longest.

prompt: Your Containerfile, copied from a tutorial, has `ENV MODEL_API_KEY=sk-...` beside `ENV PORT=8000`. What should change?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.

choices.text: The port stays; the key moves to the server's environment at run time, out of the image.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing: the image is built on the server itself and is not pushed anywhere.
choices.why: The file is in the repository, and the image carries the key wherever it goes.

choices.text: Both come out of the file, since every value in the environment is a secret.

choices.text: Keep the key, and run the container as USER 1000.
choices.why: USER bounds what a bug can do; it does not hide a key.
